code.title: Pair with a given sum: nested loops vs two pointers

followUps:
Three common ones are 2-Sum on a sorted array, Container With Most Water and checking whether a string is a palindrome. In each, one pointer starts at the left end, the other at the right end, and they walk towards each other.

  • 2-Sum: move L right if the sum is too small, R left if it is too big.
  • Container: move the shorter wall inward.
  • Palindrome: compare s[L] with s[R], then move both. For "level": l=l, e=e, middle reached, so it is a palindrome.

Others: reversing an array, 3-Sum (after fixing one value) and Trapping Rain Water. All run in O(N) time (3-Sum O(N2)) and O(1) extra space.

The data must have some order, so that one comparison tells you a whole group of candidates can never be the answer. Most often this means the array is sorted.

Example: in sorted [1, 3, 4, 6, 8] with target 7, the first check is 1 + 8 = 9, too big. Because 1 is the smallest value, 8 is too big with every partner, so throwing 8 away is safe. In an unsorted array [8, 1, 6, 3, 4] you cannot say that: a smaller partner may be anywhere, so a pointer move could skip the real answer.

The order does not have to come from sorting. In Container With Most Water it comes from the width, which only shrinks as pointers move inward. The rule is the same: only discard what you can prove is useless.

code.title: 2-Sum on a sorted array: trace every pointer move
code.python:
a = [2, 5, 7, 9, 12, 16]   # sorted
target = 16
print(f"array: {a} target: {target}")
L, R = 0, len(a) - 1
found = False
# Time O(N): each step moves one pointer inward. Space O(1).
while L < R:
    s = a[L] + a[R]
    line = f"L={L} R={R} sum={s}"
    if s == target:
        print(f"{line} -> found {a[L]} + {a[R]}")
        found = True
        break
    elif s > target:
        # a[R] is too big even with the smallest value left, so drop it
        print(line + " too big, move R left")
        R -= 1
    else:
        # a[L] is too small even with the biggest value left, so drop it
        print(line + " too small, move L right")
        L += 1
if not found:
    print("no pair")

followUps:
No. The proof only uses the fact that the array is sorted; the sign of the numbers never appears in it.

The key step is "if L is at or before the true left index, then a[L] is not bigger than the true left value". That is true for any sorted numbers, negative or not.

Example: [-5, -2, 0, 3, 8], target 1. -5 + 8 = 3, too big, so R--. -5 + 3 = -2, too small, so L++. -2 + 3 = 1, found.

Do not confuse this with sliding windows over sums, which do need non-negative numbers. Two-pointer 2-Sum is O(N) time and O(1) space for any sorted input.

Instead of stopping at one pair, you add a whole group of pairs at once: if a[L] + a[R] < target, then a[L] also works with every index between L+1 and R, because those values are no bigger than a[R]. That is R - L pairs.

int L = 0, R = n - 1, count = 0;
while (L < R) {
  if (a[L] + a[R] < target) { count += R - L; L++; }
  else R--;
}

Example: [1, 2, 3, 5], target 6. 1 + 5 = 6 is not below 6, so R--. 1 + 3 = 4: add 2 pairs, L++. 2 + 3 = 5: add 1 pair. Total 3: (1,2), (1,3), (2,3). The proof changes from "we never skip the answer" to "every pair is counted or rejected exactly once". Still O(N) time, O(1) space.

code.title: 2-Sum on an unsorted array with a hash map (keeps original indices)
code.python:
a = [8, 3, 11, 5, 2]   # not sorted, and we must report indices
target = 13
print(f"array: {a} target: {target}")
# value -> index where we saw it. Time O(N), space O(N).
seen = {}
found = False
for i, x in enumerate(a):
    need = target - x              # the partner this value needs
    if need in seen:               # partner appeared earlier
        print(f"indices {seen[need]} and {i} ({need} + {x})")
        found = True
        break
    seen[x] = i                    # store AFTER the check: no self-pairing
if not found:
    print("no pair")

followUps:
On a stream you use a hash set, because you cannot sort numbers that have not arrived yet. For each new number x, first ask "is target - x already in the set?"; if yes you have a pair, otherwise add x to the set.

Example: target 13, stream 8, 3, 11, 5. For 8 we need 5: not seen, store 8. For 3 we need 10: store 3. For 11 we need 2: store 11. For 5 we need 8: seen, so the pair is (8, 5).

Each number costs O(1) time on average. Memory is O(N) in the worst case, because any old number may be needed later. If the stream never ends you must limit memory, for example by keeping only the last W numbers (a sliding window over the stream) and removing the oldest from the set.

Store the numbers in a hash map from value to how many times it was added; add is then O(1) and find walks over the distinct values.

  1. add(x): count[x]++.
  2. find(t): for each stored value v, look for t - v. If it is a different value, it only has to exist. If it equals v, you need two copies.
boolean find(int t) {
  for (int v : count.keySet()) {
    int need = t - v;
    if (need != v ? count.containsKey(need) : count.get(v) >= 2) return true;
  }
  return false;
}

Example: after add(3), add(3), add(5): find(6) is true (3 + 3), find(10) is false (only one 5). Cost: add O(1), find O(distinct values), space O(N). If find is called far more often, store every pair sum in a set at add time: add O(N), find O(1).

code.title: 3-Sum without a hash set: sort, then skip equal neighbours
code.python:
nums = [-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4, -2, 2, 0, 0]
print(f"input:  {nums}")
nums.sort()                                  # equal values become neighbours
print(f"sorted: {nums}")
count, n = 0, len(nums)
# Time O(N^2) after the O(N log N) sort; extra space O(1).
for i in range(n - 2):
    if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]:
        continue                             # same first value: skip
    L, R = i + 1, n - 1
    while L < R:
        s = nums[i] + nums[L] + nums[R]
        if s < 0:
            L += 1
        elif s > 0:
            R -= 1
        else:
            print(f"[{nums[i]}, {nums[L]}, {nums[R]}]")
            count += 1
            # record first, THEN jump over the copies of both values
            while L < R and nums[L] == nums[L + 1]:
                L += 1
            while L < R and nums[R] == nums[R - 1]:
                R -= 1
            L += 1
            R -= 1
print(f"unique triplets: {count}")

followUps:
You lose every triplet that uses the same value twice. If you jump L over equal neighbours before checking the sum, L can never stand on the first copy while R stands on the second copy.

Example: sorted [-2, 1, 1]. Fix -2, so L is on the first 1 and R on the second 1. The correct code checks -2 + 1 + 1 = 0 and records [-2, 1, 1]. If you skip copies of nums[L] first, L moves onto R, the loop L < R ends, and the triplet is never reported. [0, 0, 0] is lost the same way.

So the order is: check and record first, and only then move past the copies of the two values you just used. Skipping after recording removes repeats; skipping before recording removes real answers.

Add one more outer loop: fix two values i and j, then run the same two pointers on the rest. Each fixed index skips a value equal to the one before it, and L/R skip copies after a hit, exactly as in 3-Sum.

for (i = 0; i < n - 3; i++) { if (i > 0 && a[i] == a[i-1]) continue;
  for (j = i + 1; j < n - 2; j++) { if (j > i + 1 && a[j] == a[j-1]) continue;
    long sum = (long) a[i] + a[j] + a[L] + a[R];   // L = j+1, R = n-1
    // move L / R as in 3-Sum
  } }

Time is O(N3), extra space O(1). The overflow risk: four values near 1,000,000,000 add up to 4,000,000,000, which is more than the largest 32-bit int (2,147,483,647). The sum wraps around to a wrong number and comparisons with the target fail. Compute the sum in a 64-bit long.

code.title: Container With Most Water: move the shorter wall, check against brute force

followUps:
In Container With Most Water you choose just two walls and the bars between them do not exist; in Trapping Rain Water every bar is solid and you add up the water standing on top of each bar.

Example [3, 1, 3]: the container answer is min(3, 3) × 2 = 6. The trapped water is only 2, because the middle bar of height 1 fills part of the space: level 3 minus height 1.

  • Container: answer is one maximum of min(h[L], h[R]) × (R - L).
  • Rain water: answer is a sum over bars of min(tallest on the left, tallest on the right) - h[i].

Both can be solved with two pointers from the ends in O(N) time and O(1) space, but rain water also keeps a running leftMax and rightMax.

When both walls have the same height you can move either one, or both; the answer stays correct.

Reason: say both walls have height 5. Any other container that keeps one of them has a smaller width and a water level of at most 5, so it cannot beat the area you just measured. That means both walls are finished, and a better container must use two new walls.

Example [5, 2, 7, 5]: the first area is min(5, 5) × 3 = 15. Keeping the left 5 gives at most 5 × 2 = 10; keeping the right 5 gives at most 5 × 2 = 10. So 15 is final whichever pointer moves.

The usual code if (h[L] < h[R]) L++; else R--; simply moves R on a tie. Moving both saves one step but does not change O(N) time.

code.title: Read/write pointers: remove duplicates and move zeroes in place
code.python:
# Keep one copy of each value in a sorted list. Time O(N), space O(1).
def dedupe(a):
    slow = 0                                  # next free cell for a kept value
    for fast in range(len(a)):                # fast reads every element once
        if slow == 0 or a[fast] != a[slow - 1]:   # keep rule: differs from last kept
            a[slow] = a[fast]
            slow += 1
    return slow                               # a[0..slow-1] is the answer


# Same template, keep rule "non-zero", then fill the tail with zeroes.
def move_zeroes(a):
    slow = 0
    for fast in range(len(a)):
        if a[fast] != 0:
            a[slow] = a[fast]
            slow += 1
    while slow < len(a):
        a[slow] = 0
        slow += 1


a = [1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 5, 5]
print(f"sorted input: {a}")
k = dedupe(a)
print(f"kept {k} values: {a[:k]}")

b = [0, 3, 0, 0, 7, 1, 0]
print(f"input: {b}")
move_zeroes(b)
print(f"zeroes moved to the end: {b}")

followUps:
Write only when a value really has to change place, and if the order of the kept elements does not matter, fill each hole with the last element instead of shifting everything.

  1. Order must be kept: skip the copy when slow == fast (the element is already in the right cell).
  2. Order is free: overwrite the removed element with the last one and shrink the length.
int i = 0, n = a.length;
while (i < n) {
  if (a[i] == val) a[i] = a[--n];   // one write per removed element
  else i++;
}

Example: remove 3 from [3, 1, 2, 5, 4]. The standard template shifts 1, 2, 5, 4 left: 4 writes. The swap version writes once: a[0] = 4, giving [4, 1, 2, 5]. Both are O(N) time and O(1) space; the second does as many writes as there are removed elements, which matters when writes are expensive.

Most languages ship this exact loop, so in real code you rarely write it by hand.

  • C++: std::remove / std::remove_if (remove element), std::unique (dedupe neighbours). They return the new end, like slow; you then call erase (the "erase-remove idiom"), or use C++20 std::erase_if.
  • Java: ArrayList.removeIf(x -> x == 0) compacts the backing array in one pass.
  • C#: List<T>.RemoveAll(predicate).
  • Python / JavaScript: a[:] = [x for x in a if x != 0] and a.filter(...) give the same result but build a new list, so they use O(N) extra space.

Example: std::unique on [1, 1, 2, 2, 3] leaves [1, 2, 3, ?, ?] and returns a pointer to index 3. All are O(N) time.

code.title: Fixed window (max sum of K items) vs variable window (shortest sum >= target)
code.python:
# Fixed size: the length K is given. Time O(N), space O(1).
def max_sum_of_k(a, k):
    s = sum(a[:k])                     # build the first window
    best = s
    for i in range(k, len(a)):
        s += a[i] - a[i - k]           # one comes in, one goes out
        best = max(best, s)
    return best


# Variable size: we search for the length. Positive numbers only.
# Time O(N), space O(1). Returns 0 if no window reaches the target.
def shortest_at_least(a, target):
    L, s, best = 0, 0, len(a) + 1
    for R in range(len(a)):
        s += a[R]                      # grow on the right
        while s >= target:             # good window: record, then shrink
            best = min(best, R - L + 1)
            s -= a[L]
            L += 1
    return 0 if best == len(a) + 1 else best


a = [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2]
print(f"fixed:    {a} K=3 -> max window sum = {max_sum_of_k(a, 3)}")
b = [2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3]
print(f"variable: {b} target=7 -> shortest length = {shortest_at_least(b, 7)}")

followUps:
"Find all anagrams of p inside s" looks variable, but an anagram of p always has exactly len(p) letters, so the window size is fixed.

Example: s = "cbaebabacd", p = "abc". Slide a window of length 3 and keep a letter count: "cba" matches at index 0, "bac" matches at index 6. Each step adds one letter and removes one letter.

The same is true for "does s contain a permutation of p" and "maximum number of vowels in any substring of length K". The clue is that the length of a valid answer is already decided by the input. Treating it as a variable window still works but adds a shrink loop you do not need. Cost: O(N) time, O(26) = O(1) space.

Record the answer at the moment the window is known to be valid and as good as it can get for the current right end.

  • Fixed window: record after each slide, once the window holds K elements (from index K−1 on).
  • Shortest flavour: record inside the while loop. The window is valid there and each shrink gives a shorter valid window, so every one of them is a candidate.
  • Longest / count flavour: record after the while loop. The loop repairs a broken window; when it ends, the window is the longest valid one ending at R.

Example, shortest sum ≥ 7 in [2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3]: at R = 3 the window [2,3,1,2] has sum 8, record 4, shrink to sum 6 and stop. Recording after the loop would measure an invalid window.

code.title: Count the real work of a grow/shrink window: at most 2N moves
code.python:
a = [4, 2, 1, 7, 8, 1, 2, 8, 1, 0]
limit = 8                      # longest window with sum <= limit
n = len(a)
print(f"array: {a} limit: {limit}")
L, s, best = 0, 0, 0
adds, removes = 0, 0           # counters for the amortised argument
# Time O(N) in total, space O(1).
for R in range(n):
    s += a[R]
    adds += 1                  # each index enters the window once
    while s > limit:           # inner loop: L only ever moves forward
        s -= a[L]
        L += 1
        removes += 1           # each index leaves at most once
    best = max(best, R - L + 1)
print(f"longest window length: {best}")
print(f"adds: {adds}, removes: {removes}")
print(f"total moves {adds + removes} <= 2N = {2 * n}, while N*N = {n * n}")

followUps:
A loop is truly O(N2) when the inner index starts again for every outer step, instead of continuing from where it stopped.

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
  for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++)     // j is reset every time
    if (a[i] + a[j] == target) count++;

For N = 10 the inner body runs 9 + 8 + … + 1 = 45 times, which is N(N−1)/2. For N = 100,000 that is about 5,000,000,000 steps.

Compare with the window: its inner pointer L is declared outside the for loop and never goes back, so over the whole run it moves at most N times. The test to apply is: "can the inner variable move backwards or restart?" If yes, multiply the loops; if no, add them.

It is used wherever one operation is occasionally slow but the slow cases are rare enough that the average stays small.

  • Dynamic arrays (ArrayList, vector, Python list): when full, the array doubles and copies everything. Appending 8 items with capacities 1, 2, 4, 8 copies 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 items in total, fewer than 8, so each append is O(1) on average.
  • Union-find with path compression and union by rank: one find may walk a long chain, but it flattens the chain, so M operations cost about O(M α(N)), and α(N) is at most 4 in practice.
  • Monotonic stack / deque: each element is pushed once and popped at most once, so N steps cost O(N).
  • Hash tables: resizing is O(N) but rare, so insert is O(1) on average.

code.title: Negative numbers break the window; prefix sums + hash map still work
code.python:
# Shortest subarray with sum >= k using a window. WRONG if negatives exist.
def window_shortest(a, k):
    L, s, best = 0, 0, len(a) + 1
    for R in range(len(a)):
        s += a[R]
        while s >= k:                  # assumes shrinking always lowers the sum
            best = min(best, R - L + 1)
            s -= a[L]
            L += 1
    return best


# Try every subarray: always right, O(N^2).
def brute_shortest(a, k):
    best = len(a) + 1
    for i in range(len(a)):
        s = 0
        for j in range(i, len(a)):
            s += a[j]
            if s >= k:
                best = min(best, j - i + 1)
    return best


# Count subarrays with sum exactly k. Time O(N), space O(N). Negatives are fine.
def count_exact(a, k):
    seen = {0: 1}                      # the empty prefix
    prefix, count = 0, 0
    for x in a:
        prefix += x
        count += seen.get(prefix - k, 0)   # earlier prefixes that fit
        seen[prefix] = seen.get(prefix, 0) + 1
    return count


a = [1, -1, 5]
k = 5
print(f"array: {a} k: {k}")
print(f"window says shortest length:  {window_shortest(a, k)}")
print(f"brute force says:             {brute_shortest(a, k)}")
print(f"subarrays with sum exactly k: {count_exact(a, k)}")

followUps:
Use prefix sums and a deque of start positions whose prefix sums are increasing. P[j] - P[i] is the sum of the subarray between positions i and j.

  1. For each j: while P[j] - P[front] >= K, record j - front and pop the front (any later j would only be longer).
  2. While P[back] >= P[j], pop the back: j is a later start with a smaller prefix, so it is always better.
  3. Push j.

Example [2, -1, 2], K = 3: P = [0, 2, 1, 3]. j=0: deque [0]. j=1: push, [0, 1]. j=2: P[1] = 2 ≥ P[2] = 1, pop it, deque [0, 2]. j=3: 3 − 0 ≥ 3, record length 3, pop; 3 − 1 = 2 is not enough; push. Answer 3.

Each index is pushed and popped at most once: O(N) time, O(N) space.

Ask one question before coding: "if I add an element, can the window only get worse (or only get better)?" If adding can sometimes help and sometimes hurt, the window is not safe.

Quick checks:

  • Read the constraints. Values that can be negative (for sums) or zero/negative (for products) break it.
  • The word "exactly" is a warning; "at most" and "at least" are usually fine.
  • Try a 3-element counter-example by hand. [1, -1, 5] with "shortest sum ≥ 5": the window reaches sum 5 at length 3, removes the 1, gets 4 and stops, reporting 3. The real answer is 1, the single 5.

If the check fails, say so and switch to prefix sums with a hash map or a monotonic deque. This takes under a minute and saves a wrong solution.

code.title: Exactly K distinct values = atMost(K) - atMost(K-1)
code.python:
# Number of subarrays with at most k distinct values (values are 0..9).
# Time O(N), space O(1) because the count array has a fixed size.
def at_most(a, k):
    freq = [0] * 10
    L, distinct, total = 0, 0, 0
    for R in range(len(a)):
        if freq[a[R]] == 0:
            distinct += 1              # a new value entered
        freq[a[R]] += 1
        while distinct > k:            # too many: shrink from the left
            freq[a[L]] -= 1
            if freq[a[L]] == 0:
                distinct -= 1
            L += 1
        total += R - L + 1   # every start from L to R gives a valid subarray ending at R
    return total


a = [1, 2, 1, 2, 3]
k = 2
print(f"array: {a} K: {k}")
up_to, below = at_most(a, k), at_most(a, k - 1)
print(f"atMost({k}) = {up_to}")
print(f"atMost({k - 1}) = {below}")
# "exactly K" is what is left after removing "K-1 or fewer"
print(f"exactly {k} distinct = {up_to - below}")

followUps:
Because every subarray has exactly one right end, and we count it only at the step where R is that right end.

For a fixed R, after the shrink loop L is the smallest start that keeps the window valid. Making a valid window shorter keeps it valid (fewer elements cannot add distinct values), so the valid starts are exactly L, L+1, …, R. That is R - L + 1 subarrays, all ending at R, all different.

Example [1, 2, 3], at most 2 distinct. R=0: L=0, add 1 ([1]). R=1: L=0, add 2 ([1,2], [2]). R=2: L moves to 1, add 2 ([2,3], [3]). Total 5; the only subarray not counted is [1,2,3], which has 3 distinct values. Nothing is counted twice, because two different steps have different right ends.

Keep a count of zeros in the window; when it goes above K, move L right until a zero leaves.

int atMost(int[] a, int k) {
  if (k < 0) return 0;
  int L = 0, zeros = 0, total = 0;
  for (int R = 0; R < a.length; R++) {
    if (a[R] == 0) zeros++;
    while (zeros > k) if (a[L++] == 0) zeros--;
    total += R - L + 1; }
  return total; }

Example [1, 0, 1, 0], K = 1: R=0 adds 1, R=1 adds 2, R=2 adds 3. At R=3 there are 2 zeros, so L moves to 2 and we add 2. Total 8. Check: there are 10 subarrays and 2 of them ([0,1,0] and the whole array) hold two zeros.

The k < 0 guard matters when you call atMost(K - 1) with K = 0. Time O(N), space O(1).

code.title: Trapping Rain Water with two pointers and O(1) memory
code.python:
# Time O(N), space O(1): no prefix-max or suffix-max arrays.
def trap(h):
    L, R = 0, len(h) - 1
    left_max = right_max = water = 0
    while L < R:
        if h[L] < h[R]:
            # a wall at least as tall as left_max exists on the right,
            # so the water level above bar L is decided by left_max alone
            left_max = max(left_max, h[L])
            water += left_max - h[L]
            L += 1
        else:
            # mirror case: bar R is decided by right_max alone
            right_max = max(right_max, h[R])
            water += right_max - h[R]
            R -= 1
    return water


tests = [[0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 2, 1], [4, 2, 0, 3, 2, 5], [1, 2, 3]]
for h in tests:
    print(f"heights: {h} -> water: {trap(h)}")

followUps:
Keep a stack of bar indices whose heights go down; when a taller bar arrives, it closes a "bowl", and you fill that bowl one horizontal layer at a time.

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
  while (!st.isEmpty() && h[i] > h[st.peek()]) {
    int bottom = st.pop(); if (st.isEmpty()) break;
    int left = st.peek();
    water += (Math.min(h[left], h[i]) - h[bottom]) * (i - left - 1);
  }
  st.push(i); }

Example [3, 0, 2]: push 0, push 1. At i = 2, height 2 > 0: pop the bottom (index 1), left wall is index 0, level min(3, 2) = 2, width 1, so water += 2. Answer 2.

Each index is pushed and popped once: O(N) time, O(N) space. The two-pointer version uses O(1) space, so the stack is mostly useful when you want to practise the pattern.

In 2D, water can leak out in four directions, so two pointers are not enough; you work inward from the border with a min-heap (priority queue).

  1. Put every border cell in the heap and mark it visited. Border cells hold no water.
  2. Pop the lowest cell; its height is the current water level of the "wall".
  3. For each unvisited neighbour: if it is lower, add level - height water. Push it with height max(level, height).

Example: a 3 × 3 grid with border cells of height 3 and a centre of height 1. The lowest border cell (3) is popped, the centre is its neighbour, and it gains 3 − 1 = 2 units.

Always expanding from the lowest wall is what guarantees the level is right. Cost: O(M·N·log(M·N)) time and O(M·N) space for an M × N grid.

code.title: Sliding-window rate limiter: at most 3 requests in any 10 seconds
code.python:
from collections import deque

limit, window_sec = 3, 10
times = [1, 2, 3, 5, 11, 12, 13, 14, 25]   # request times in seconds
print(f"limit: {limit} requests per {window_sec} s")
print(f"request times: {times}")
# The queue holds the times of accepted requests still inside the window.
# Time O(1) amortised per request, space O(limit).
recent = deque()
for t in times:
    # left edge of the window moves forward: drop requests that are too old
    while recent and recent[0] <= t - window_sec:
        recent.popleft()
    if len(recent) < limit:
        recent.append(t)                   # right edge: the new request enters
        print(f"t={t} ALLOW (in window: {len(recent)})")
    else:
        print(f"t={t} DENY  (in window: {len(recent)})")

followUps:
Keep a tiny amount of state per user in a shared in-memory store (such as Redis), and do not store every request time: store two counters instead.

The "sliding window counter" keeps the count for the current minute and for the previous minute, then estimates: previous × (part of the old minute still inside the window) + current.

Example: limit 100 per minute, previous minute 80, current minute 30, and we are 15 s into this minute. 75% of the old minute is still in the window: 80 × 0.75 + 30 = 90, below 100, so allow.

  • O(1) time per request and two numbers per user, so 1M users need only a few tens of MB.
  • Do the read-and-increment as one atomic step (one script) so two servers cannot both pass.
  • Give each key an expiry time so idle users disappear.

An exact log of timestamps costs O(limit) memory per user.

They drift because a floating-point number keeps only about 16 significant digits, so each add and each subtract is rounded a little, and in a running sum those small errors never get cancelled.

Example with doubles: 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004. Subtract 0.2 and you get 0.10000000000000003, not 0.1. After millions of "add new, subtract old" updates, the total can be visibly wrong; it is worse when a huge value passes through the window and wipes out the small digits.

Common fixes:

  • Use integers (store cents or microseconds instead of fractions).
  • Recompute the sum from the buffer every so often, for example each time the ring buffer wraps around.
  • Use Kahan (compensated) summation, which carries the lost error in a second variable.

code.title: Check a window solution against brute force on many small inputs
code.python:
seed = 7


# Tiny fixed random generator, so every run produces the same tests.
def nxt():
    global seed
    seed = (seed * 75 + 74) % 65537
    return seed


# Window: longest subarray with sum <= k (positive numbers). Time O(N), space O(1).
def fast(a, k):
    L, s, best = 0, 0, 0
    for R in range(len(a)):
        s += a[R]
        while s > k:               # safe only because all values are positive
            s -= a[L]
            L += 1
        best = max(best, R - L + 1)
    return best


# Every subarray. Time O(N^2). Slow but obviously right.
def brute(a, k):
    best = 0
    for i in range(len(a)):
        s = 0
        for j in range(i, len(a)):
            s += a[j]
            if s <= k:
                best = max(best, j - i + 1)
    return best


tests, mismatches = 200, 0
for t in range(tests):
    n = nxt() % 8 + 1                          # length 1..8
    a = [nxt() % 9 + 1 for _ in range(n)]      # values 1..9
    k = nxt() % 20 + 1
    f, b = fast(a, k), brute(a, k)
    if t == 0:
        print(f"sample: {a} k={k} window={f} brute={b}")
    if f != b:
        mismatches += 1                        # a mismatch would expose a bug
print(f"tests: {tests}, mismatches: {mismatches}")

followUps:
"Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock" is one: you want a pair of days, but the buy day must come before the sell day, and sorting would destroy that order.

Example: prices [7, 1, 5, 3, 6]. The right answer is 5 (buy at 1, sell at 6). If you sorted, you would pair 1 with 7 and report 6, but 7 comes before 1, so that trade is impossible.

Instead, walk once and keep the lowest price seen so far: profit = current price − lowest so far. O(N) time, O(1) space.

Other cases: 2-Sum that must return original indices (use a hash map, or sort (value, index) pairs), and counting inversions (pairs i < j with a[i] > a[j]). The rule: if the answer depends on positions, sorting plain values loses information you need.

Run the code by hand on one small input, then on the edge cases, and compare with what a brute-force check would give.

  1. Dry run: pick 4 to 6 elements and write L, R and the window state after each step. For "longest sum ≤ 8" on [4, 2, 1, 7]: windows [4], [4,2], [4,2,1], then 14 > 8 so shrink to [7]. Answer 3.
  2. Edge cases: empty input, one element, all equal values, answer at the very start or end, no valid answer.
  3. Invariant: say in one sentence what is true after each step and check the first and last step against it.
  4. Off-by-one: length is R - L + 1; loops use L < R for pairs.
  5. Cost: confirm each pointer only moves forward, so the time is O(N).

With a computer, generate small random arrays and compare against the O(N2) version.
